scenarios.name: 3 players: the 3-card favour deck is fully dealt, one card each
4 players: 6-card favour deck, 4 dealt, 2 remain
At start every pile is 0 and nothing is built
Market gain changes a private stock that enables only the owner to build
Round begins: round becomes 1 and bonus is drawn from the locations list
Refill: each pile +3, bonus Forest gets +5
Talk step runs for all and the round completes
Gather choice offers all seven options and choices are public
Wolf at Fields: gatherer gets nothing and pile unchanged
5 straw split by 2: each gets 2, 1 stays
Unchosen piles carry over
All choose Market: each gains 1 favoured and builds it at cost 1
Wolf chooser gains nothing and can build nothing
Lone gatherers empty their piles; choices and piles public (bonus-independent)
Favoured section costs 1, other costs 2
Build adds to the unfinished house, or starts a new one at the Floor
Roof completes the house: done +1, completed +1, progress back to 0
No third house of a material, and unaffordable builds are not offered
Building a section adds 1 to sections
Exactly 2 build actions per round even with stock for more
Third completed house sets finished and ends the game after the round
Single finisher wins over a non-finisher with more leftovers
Two finishers: most leftover materials wins
Two finishers with equal leftovers share the win
Round 15 ends with no finisher: most completed, then sections
Round 15 ends with a full tie at the top: shared win

spec_choices.why: The designer suggests 3 and the deal is defined for 3 and 4. At 3, the favoured materials are a perfect split, so guessing the others' materials is clean deduction, and contesting a pile or sending the Wolf has a clear target. A fifth player has no deal defined, and splitting the piles that many ways would leave almost no gains.

spec_choices.what: Talk kept as one simultaneous poll per round, broadcast to all
spec_choices.why: The source requires it. Players disagree: each wants a pile to themselves and wants to hide their favoured material. Bluffing about where you will go, or threatening a Wolf, gives everyone something to reason about. The talk is simultaneous because the source says messages are written at the same time.

spec_choices.what: Build offers include only legal builds, plus Pass
spec_choices.why: A seat is never offered what it may not do. The 'counts as Pass' rule stays as a backstop. The filter uses only the seat's own private stockpile, so it leaks nothing.

spec_choices.what: Ranking expression: finisher offset 100000, completed weight 100
spec_choices.why: A non-finisher's value is at most 2*100 + 12 sections, well below 100000, so finishers always rank above everyone. The weight of 100 makes completed houses outrank sections, since sections never reach 100.

spec_choices.what: Sections tie-break counts every section ever built, including those in completed houses
spec_choices.why: The source says 'most built sections' without restricting it.

spec_choices.what: Gather and wolf counts are announced after resolution
spec_choices.why: The source says the piles and the number of gatherers are public, so anyone can work out each gain.

simplifications.what: Each house is tracked as a progress counter (0-2) plus a completed count per material, not as a list of named sections
simplifications.why: Floor, Walls and Roof are always built in order, so a counter holds the same information.

simplifications.what: The 'one unfinished house per material' rule is enforced by the build always adding to the existing unfinished house
simplifications.why: The engine has no separate choice to start a second unfinished house, so the limit holds automatically.

variation.original_summary: The Grimm Forest is a 2-4 player race in which the three little pigs secretly choose where to gather straw, wood or brick. A pig alone at a location takes all of its resources, while pigs who share a location split them. Players then spend materials to build houses floor, then walls, then roof, using Fable and Friend cards to interfere, and the first to finish three houses wins.

review.evidence: Simultaneous location choice with a split when players share punishes any fixed policy. A player who always picks the same location is easy to read, gets shared or blocked by Monsters, and the others can avoid them or crowd them. Turn order gives the first player a small edge in Fables and building, but the core choice is a fair simultaneous one.
Guessing where others will go and timing builds is real skill. However, the Fable and Friend draws are large swings that come from the deck, and a lucky Fable can wipe out a well-read gather round.
Reading opponents' needs from their half-built houses, exploiting piles of leftover resources and timing the finish all reward deeper play. A weak player still gathers and builds something.
Gather cards are secret and simultaneous, so you must predict who goes where. Fables are hidden, and what a player needs can be inferred from their houses.
Splitting, building costs and the three-house finish are all arithmetic, so no judge is needed.

The Fable deck has dozens of unique effects and Monster miniatures. Friend cards carry once-per-turn special powers, players build in turn order, and a player can force a card onto another. Far more cards and rules exist than the step and attribute limits allow, even though the core loop is text-friendly.

problems: The Fable deck (many unique effects) and the Friend cards (individual powers, forced gifting) far exceed the platform's step, attribute and hidden-element limits.
Fable and Friend draws add large luck swings that can override good gather-reading.
Building in turn order and resolving Fables in turn order give seat-dependent advantages.
With any combination of houses allowed and all materials worth the same to everyone, players have no private agenda to hide or infer. The only inference is from public board state.
There is no turn cap or tiebreak for simultaneous finishes, which a fixed-length engine needs.

changes.what: Replace the whole Fable deck with one Wolf gather option: instead of gathering, a player sends the Wolf to a location. Nobody gathers there this round, and the pile stays and grows.
changes.why: This keeps the Monster idea of scaring pigs off a location as a single arithmetic rule. It also gives a way to block a leader or punish a predictable opponent, at the cost of your own gathering.
changes.fixes: The Fable deck (many unique effects) and the Friend cards (individual powers, forced gifting) far exceed the platform's step, attribute and hidden-element limits.

changes.what: Remove Friend cards and the draw-a-Fable build action.
changes.why: This cuts complexity and removes card luck, so outcomes come from gather choices and build timing.
changes.fixes: Fable and Friend draws add large luck swings that can override good gather-reading.

changes.what: All choices (gather, and both build actions) are simultaneous polls. Ties for the win are broken by leftover resources, not seat.
changes.fixes: Building in turn order and resolving Fables in turn order give seat-dependent advantages.

changes.what: Deal each player a secret Favoured Material, for which each section costs 1 instead of 2. Keep each player's stockpile private. Allow at most 2 completed houses of any one material, so every winner needs at least one house in a non-favoured material.
changes.why: This gives every player a hidden agenda. Others must infer your type from where you gather and what you build, and stockpiles cannot be reconstructed without knowing your costs. The two-per-material cap forces everyone into a contested second material, so collisions and Wolf blocks are real decisions.
changes.fixes: With any combination of houses allowed and all materials worth the same to everyone, players have no private agenda to hide or infer. The only inference is from public board state.

changes.what: Set a 15-round cap. If several players finish on the same round, the one with most leftover resources wins. At the cap, compare most houses, then most sections, else draw.
changes.fixes: There is no turn cap or tiebreak for simultaneous finishes, which a fixed-length engine needs.

changes.what: Add one random bonus each round (+2 to one announced location) and a non-shared Market giving 1 of your favoured material.
changes.why: The bonus plays the role of the original's Mega resources, a public lure that creates collisions. The Market preserves the 4-player location as a safe but slow option. Both are publicly known before players choose, so they shape decisions rather than decide outcomes.
changes.fixes: Fable and Friend draws add large luck swings that can override good gather-reading.

keeps: A secret, simultaneous gather location choice among Fields (straw), Forest (wood) and Brickyard (brick), plus a Market.
Alone you take the whole pile, shared you split it rounding down, and leftovers stay and accumulate.
Houses built section by section: floor, then walls, then roof, paid in that house's material, with only one unfinished house per material.
Monsters scaring pigs away from a location (the Wolf).
A race: the first to complete three houses wins.

recommendation.reason: The core gather-collision and build-race loop is simultaneous, arithmetic and inference-rich. Only the card decks are too heavy, and they can be replaced by one Wolf rule and a hidden favoured material.

variation.name: Three Pigs: Secret Materials
variation.summary: 3-4 pigs secretly pick where to gather each round. They split piles when they share, can send the Wolf to spoil a location, and race to build three houses. Each pig's cheap material is secret, and nobody can win with one material alone.
variation.rules:
SETUP
- Materials: Straw, Wood, Brick.
- Locations: Fields (Straw), Forest (Wood), Brickyard (Brick). Each starts with a pile of 0.
- Each player is secretly dealt a Favoured Material:
  - 3 players: shuffle one Straw, one Wood and one Brick card and deal one each, so all three differ.
  - 4 players: shuffle two each of Straw, Wood and Brick and deal one each.
- A player's Favoured Material is known only to them.
- Each player starts with 0 Straw, 0 Wood and 0 Brick. A player's stockpile is private, known only to them.

HOUSES
- A house is one material and has three sections, built in order: Floor, Walls, Roof.
- Each section costs 2 of that house's material, or 1 if it is the builder's Favoured Material.
- A player may have at most one unfinished house of each material.
- A player may complete at most 2 houses of any one material.
- Which sections each player has built, and of what material, is public. The cost paid is not shown.

EACH ROUND (up to 15 rounds)
1. Bonus: one location is drawn at random (each 1/3) and announced.
2. Refill: every location's pile gains 3, and the announced location gains 2 more.
3. Talk: everyone writes one short message at the same time, then all messages are shown to everyone. Messages bind no one.
4. Gather choice: everyone simultaneously chooses one of seven options:
   - Fields, Forest, Brickyard, Market;
   - Wolf-Fields, Wolf-Forest, Wolf-Brickyard.
5. Reveal: all choices are shown.
6. Resolve each of the three locations:
   - If any player chose Wolf at that location, nobody gathers there and its pile is unchanged.
   - Otherwise, the pile is divided equally among the players who chose it, rounding down. Each takes their share of that material, and the remainder stays in the pile.
   - If nobody chose the location, the pile stays.
   - Each player is told only their own gain, but the piles and the number of gatherers are public, so gains can be computed by anyone.
7. Market: every player who chose Market gains 1 of their Favoured Material. Any number of players can use the Market without sharing.
8. Players who chose a Wolf gain nothing.
9. Build action 1: everyone simultaneously chooses Build Straw, Build Wood, Build Brick or Pass.
   - A build adds the next section to that player's house of that material, starting a new house at the Floor if none is unfinished, and pays the cost from their stockpile.
   - If the player cannot pay, or the build would start a third house of that material, it counts as Pass.
   - The resulting public build state is shown.
10. Build action 2: exactly as build action 1.
11. Win check: any player with 3 completed houses has finished.
    - If exactly one player has finished, they win.
    - If several have, the finisher with the most total leftover resources wins. If that is tied, it is a draw among them.
    - The game then ends.
12. If round 15 ends with no finisher, the game ends. The winner is the player with the most completed houses, then the most built sections. If still tied, it is a draw.
variation.objective: The first player to complete 3 houses (at most 2 of any one material) wins. If several do so in the same round, the one with the most leftover resources wins, and a further tie is a draw. If nobody finishes in 15 rounds, the winner is the player with the most completed houses, then the most sections. Any remaining tie is a draw.
variation.expected_effect:
Every simple policy loses.
- Always Market gains only the Favoured Material, so it can never build the required non-favoured house.
- Always one location gains one material only, so it caps at 2 houses.
- Always Wolf never gathers.
- Random play wastes rounds on collisions and Wolves.

Good play means:
- inferring each rival's Favoured Material from where they gather and which houses they build;
- predicting which piles they will avoid or crowd, and timing a raid on a big accumulated pile;
- using the Wolf to stall whoever is closest to finishing.

With 3 players the types are a permutation, so identifying one rival's type narrows the others. Because the materials are symmetric and the types are worth the same, the deal changes what to do rather than who wins.

Talk earns its place because only one player can win:
- Players may propose splitting locations ('I'll take Forest, you take Fields'), claim false types, or call for a Wolf on the leader.
- A player who simply follows a proposal can walk into a collision, leave a big pile to a rival who lied, or Wolf a location in a way that hands the race to the proposer.
- They disagree about who gathers which contested material and whom to block.

balanced.evidence:
COST TABLE. Each house is 3 sections. A section costs 1 in your Favoured Material and 2 otherwise. You may complete at most 2 houses of one material, so finishing needs at least 6 Favoured sections (6 units) plus 3 non-Favoured sections (6 units of one other material): 12 units and 9 sections. With 2 build actions per round, the fastest finish is round 5.

SUPPLY. Piles gain 3+3+3+2 = 11 per round, about 3.67 per location. Gathering alone at a pile yields 3 to 5 or more. Sharing between two yields 1 or 2. Market always yields 1 Favoured unit, cannot be blocked and is never shared. Wolf yields 0.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (winner rule applied):
(a) Always Market, build when able. Gets 15 Favoured units but no other material, so it caps at 2 houses and 6 sections (reached by about round 6) and can never finish. Against sensible players who gather alone they reach 6 sections by about round 3 and finish by about rounds 6 to 9, so it LOSES. If the game stalls to round 15, any sensible player with 2 houses and 1 or more third-house sections out-ranks it, so it LOSES again. It usually beats purely random players, which is acceptable.
(b) Always the first option (Fields), build when able. Gets only Straw, so it caps at 2 Straw houses and 6 sections. Every single-location policy has this same cap. It LOSES to sensible play by the first-finish rule or the section tiebreak.
(c) Always the last option (Wolf-Brickyard). Gains 0 and builds 0, so it LOSES to everyone, including random players.
(d) Always Pass on builds. Has 0 sections and LOSES.
No policy is never-losing.

DOMINANCE. Gather and Market are not ranked the same way in every case: alone at a location beats Market (3 or more against 1); a crowded or wolfed location is worse than Market (0 to 1 against 1). Wolf has a payoff only against an opponent, at a cost of 0 gain to yourself, and the blocked pile grows by 3 or more each round, so a skipped Wolf hands a big payout to whoever is waiting. Wolfing is a mutual guessing game, not a dominant option. No option is strictly best whatever the opponents do.

SEATS. All choices are simultaneous and there is no turn order, so there is no seat edge. A same-round tie goes to leftover resources, which is arithmetic.

3-PLAYER DEAL. The three Favoured Materials are distinct and the structure is symmetric.

4-PLAYER DEAL. The deal is 4 cards from {S,S,W,W,B,B}: a 2-1-1 pattern in 36 of 54 ordered deals and 2-2-0 in 18 of 54. In two-thirds of 4-player games, two players share a Favoured pile (about 1.8 each against about 3.7 alone). That is a real but moderate edge. It can be overcome because every player must roam for 6 non-Favoured units, which contests all piles. Sharing is also inferable from public gains and builds, and paired players can switch to Market, other piles or Wolf the unique players.

CONCLUSION. Every player can realistically win, and no labelled payoff ordering is contradicted. Pass, with the 4-player pairing as the weakest point.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE SOURCES. There are two:
(1) The bonus location (+2, each 1/3). It is announced BEFORE choices, so it is information to act on, and a crowd at the bonus pile can split it to nothing.
(2) The Favoured deal. It is symmetric in 3-player games. In 4-player games it is moderately asymmetric in 2/3 of deals, as shown above.
I estimate chance at about 15 to 25% of results in 4-player games and about 10% in 3-player games.

INFERENCE. All gathering gains are computable from public piles and choices, so opponents' location income is effectively public. What stays hidden is the type of each Market gain and the Favoured Material. Favoured Material is deducible from build timing: a section built with only 1 unit of a material on hand reveals it, and in 3-player games the materials are distinct, so one deduction constrains the others.

ACTING ON IT. Players can:
- predict where opponents will gather, avoiding splits or targeting them with a Wolf;
- see from the public build state which non-Favoured material a leader still needs, and Wolf that location;
- guess, as the leader, when the blocker will relent and the hoarded pile pays out;
- time builds and hoard leftovers for the same-round tiebreak.

ALL PLAY WELL. With equal good play in 3-player games, the winner comes from the pile-contest and Wolf guessing, not from the draw. In 4-player games the deal tilts the game but does not decide it, because non-Favoured supply is contested by everyone. A reasoning player is clearly favoured over a careless one, who over-crowds piles, Wolfs aimlessly or tries to finish from a single location.
